title: Chapter XXIV

teacherSummary.text: Caroline's letter confirms the Bingleys will stay in London. Jane bears it quietly. Elizabeth reflects bitterly on the 'inconsistency of all human characters.' Mr. Bennet jokes that Wickham would make a fine jilt.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXIV,” how does Austen show disappointment and philosophy? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXIV develops the idea of disappointment and philosophy. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXIV to complicate the reader's understanding of disappointment and philosophy. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXIV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of disappointment and philosophy responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXIV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of disappointment and philosophy. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: Hope was over, entirely over; and when Jane could attend to the rest of the letter, she found little, except the professed affection of the writer, that could give her any comfort. Miss Darcy’s praise occupied the chief of it. Her many attractions were again dwelt on, and Caroline boasted joyfully of their increasing intimacy, and ventured to predict the accomplishment of the wishes which had been unfolded in her former letter. She wrote also with great pleasure of her brother’s being an inmate of Mr. Darcy’s house, and mentioned with raptures, some plans of the latter with regard to new furniture.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XXIV”?

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: How does Jane's restraint compare with Elizabeth's response? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include disclaimed, extenuating, unreserve, encroaching, confirms. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Miss Bennet eagerly disclaimed all extraordinary merit, and threw back the praise on her sister’s warm affection.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To renounce all claim to deny.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Women's feelings were expected to be hidden for propriety. Now, why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's cynicism shows how disappointment shapes judgment. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
